articles.title: [Bilateral serous chorioretinopathy under immune checkpoint treatment- : Diagnostic dilemma in possible bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation (BDUMP) in lymphatic metastasized chromophobe renal cell carcinoma].
articles.abstract: Bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation (BDUMP) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by pigmentary and angiographic abnormalities, choroidal thickening, and serous retinal detachments. In patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, differentiation from immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated serous chorioretinopathy may be particularly challenging. We report the case of a 55-year-old patient with lymphogenically metastatic chromophobe renal cell carcinoma receiving nivolumab and ipilimumab who developed progressive bilateral visual loss and multiple choroidal pigmentary changes. Multimodal imaging revealed bilateral serous detachments of the neurosensory retina, subretinal hyperreflective material, and exudative macular changes. The constellation of findings initially raised suspicion of BDUMP. However, a definitive diagnosis could not be established because essential investigations, including EDI-OCT, B-scan ultrasonography, and adequately documented assessment were unavailable. At the same time, immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated serous chorioretinopathy remained an important differential diagnosis. During continued immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, the exudative changes progressed markedly over three months, accompanied by a decline in visual acuity to 0.1 in both eyes. This case illustrates the diagnostic dilemma between BDUMP and immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated serous chorioretinopathy. The available findings do not permit a definitive distinction, and the clinical course is not diagnostically discriminatory. Comprehensive multimodal imaging and close interdisciplinary collaboration are essential for diagnostic assessment.

articles.title: Spatial architecture shapes programmed cell death-associated immune niches and therapeutic resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by VHL-HIF pathway alterations, lipid remodeling, abnormal angiogenesis, and marked immune heterogeneity. These features create a highly vascular yet unevenly perfused microenvironment in which vascular dysfunction, hypoxia, stromal barriers, and myeloid clearance influence whether cell death becomes immunologically productive. Although immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and HIF-2α inhibitors have improved outcomes, primary and acquired resistance and discordant responses among lesions remain common. Bulk PD-L1 expression, immune-cell abundance, and cell-death-related transcript signatures do not resolve this heterogeneity. Following current nomenclature, regulated cell death (RCD) is the mechanistically preferred umbrella term; we retain programmed cell death (PCD) in the conceptual label because it remains widely used in the RCC oncology literature, while requiring RCD execution-level evidence for mechanistic claims. Single-cell and spatial multi-omics studies increasingly show that the identity of the dying cell, execution of the death program, accessibility of death-derived material, and the recipient immune cells operate as a coupled local system. We define a PCD-associated immune niche as a spatial tissue state in which representative, non-exclusive immune-routing axes can direct tumor-cell death toward cDC1-mediated cross-presentation and adaptive antitumor immunity, TAM-dominant efferocytosis and tissue repair, or intermediate mixed states. This Review focuses predominantly on ccRCC, evaluates ferroptosis, apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and PANoptosis, and briefly considers emerging RCD modalities for which ccRCC evidence is less mature. We further propose composite spatial biomarkers and mechanism-guided combinations that link cellular source, execution evidence, immune routing, and clinical outcome.

articles.title: IV Vitamin C with Chemotherapy for Cisplatin-Ineligible Bladder Cancer Patients: A Forgotten Group.
articles.abstract: Purpose: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy (NAC) is considered the standard of care (SOC) for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). However, approximately 50% of patients are cisplatin-ineligible (CI) and often proceed directly to surgery. We initiated a phase Ib/IIa trial to evaluate high-dose intravenous ascorbate (IVC) with gemcitabine/carboplatin (Gem/Carbo) as NAC for patients with CI-MIBC (NCT04046094). Patients and Methods: Patients with newly diagnosed CI-MIBC received a single cycle of Gem (1000 mg/m2 D1, 8)/Carbo (AUC 5 d 1) and IVC (25-125 g titrated to 350-400 mg/dL blood concentrations 2 × per week for 21 days) followed by definitive cystectomy. The primary outcome was pathological downstaging (Results: Sixteen participants were enrolled, and 12 completed the protocol. The mean age was 76. Pathological downstaging was present in four patients (33%), with 3/4 patients having a pathologic complete response (pCR, ypT0N0Mx). The treatment was well tolerated. At a mean follow-up of 32.3 months (SD 18.9, range 6.6-63.8), four patients without response recurred and died of disease, and three with response had recurred, with one passing from disease. The QOL FACT-Bl did not change from baseline to the end of treatment to 6 weeks post-cystectomy. Conclusions: Neoadjuvant, single-cycle Gem/Carbo + IVC had significant activity in patients with CI-MIBC with a response rate (RR) comparable to historical outcomes of SOC therapy in this early-phase trial. Larger trials are warranted to confirm these findings and to identify biomarkers for response.

articles.title: Urinary Metabolomics in Bladder Cancer: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence and Translation Implications.
articles.abstract: Bladder cancer (BC) diagnosis and surveillance currently rely largely on invasive cystoscopy, making urine an attractive non-invasive biofluid for discovering metabolic biomarkers, given its direct contact with the bladder urothelium. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of the literature on urinary metabolomic profiling in BC, summarising metabolites and metabolite panels associated with the disease, their relevant metabolic pathways, and diagnostic performance. A search was conducted in PubMed, complemented by records from reference lists of relevant reviews. After screening, 30 original studies comparing urinary metabolomic profiles between BC patients and cancer-free controls were included, encompassing diverse analytical platforms and statistical approaches. A wide range of urinary metabolites were reported to be altered between BC patients and controls, of which 52 were recurrently identified in at least two independent studies. Increased levels of taurine, valine, lactate, adenosine monophosphate and adipate were among the most consistent metabolic alterations, whereas the levels of citrate, glycerol, creatinine, and several dicarboxylic acids and acylcarnitines were consistently decreased. Other metabolites, such as hippurate, tyrosine, and histidine, showed variable trends in their levels. These alterations may reflect metabolic processes associated with tumour growth, energy reprogramming, lipid metabolism, and oxidative stress adaptation. Most studies also proposed multi-metabolite panels combining metabolites to discriminate BC patients from controls, achieving sensitivity and specificity up to 100% and AUC up to 0.983, while fewer studies explored panels for tumour stage and grade discrimination, with more modest performance. Overall, urinary metabolomics reveals a broad, biologically coherent set of metabolic alterations associated with BC, but methodological heterogeneity and limited independent validation still hinder clinical translation. Larger, harmonised, prospectively validated studies integrating multi-omics and machine learning are needed to establish robust urinary biomarkers for BC.

articles.title: USP30 Beyond Mitophagy: A Context-Dependent Deubiquitinase in Cancer Progression.
articles.abstract: Ubiquitin-specific protease 30 (USP30) is a mitochondrial outer membrane-associated deubiquitinase best known for antagonizing PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-dependent ubiquitination and suppressing mitophagy. This established role has linked USP30 to mitochondrial quality control and neurodegenerative diseases. However, emerging studies in cancer have expanded the biological scope of USP30, revealing functions that cannot be explained by mitophagy regulation alone. USP30 regulates diverse cancer-associated substrates through deubiquitination, thereby affecting protein abundance, subcellular localization, protein interactions, and downstream transcriptional programs. These substrate-dependent effects influence mitochondrial dynamics, lipid synthesis, glucose and amino acid metabolism, redox homeostasis, apoptosis, ferroptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stemness, T-cell exhaustion, and therapy resistance. Although most studies indicate tumor-promoting roles of USP30 in hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, ovarian cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, and leukemia models, context-dependent tumor-restraining activities have also been reported. In this Review, we examine cancer-associated functions of USP30 that extend beyond its established role in PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy, discuss the spatial and substrate-dependent mechanisms underlying these activities, and highlight opportunities and challenges for therapeutic targeting.

articles.title: Targeting Branched-Chain Amino Acid Transamination Sensitizes Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma to Glutaminase Inhibition.
articles.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a well-described hallmark of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). Gene copy number variation and altered gene expression data suggest enhanced branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) transamination and reduced BCAA oxidation are highly selected traits in ccRCC. Surprisingly, we found that genetic modulation of BCAA oxidation had little effect on experimental ccRCC cell growth in vitro and in vivo. In contrast, BCAA transamination in ccRCC cells was essential for the generation of glutamate-derived glutathione and cell viability when glutamine was limiting. Thus, BCAA transamination conferred resistance to states of low glutamine or treatment with the glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 by providing glutathione independent of glutamine breakdown. Targeting BCAA transamination in vitro and in vivo sensitized ccRCC to CB-839 mediated glutaminase inhibition by decreasing glutathione biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. These findings reveal that BCAA transamination maintains critical glutamate and glutathione levels in glutamine-deprived ccRCC, explaining why CB-839 treatment has been ineffective in ccRCC clinical trials and demonstrate an approach to treat ccRCC by targeting BCAA transamination to create a vulnerability to glutaminase inhibition.

articles.title: Pazopanib alternating with bevacizumab in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma naive to treatment: a multicentre, single-arm, phase 1/2 trial.
articles.abstract: VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are considered the backbone for the treatment of metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. We hypothesise that the administration of bevacizumab during scheduled breaks in pazopanib (TKI) treatment can improve tolerability and prolong progression-free survival compared with historical controls. In this single-arm, phase 1/2 trial in five US academic cancer centres, patients (aged ≥18 years) with histologically confirmed metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and adequate organ functions were included. The phase 1 portion included patients with up to one previous therapy with high-dose IL-2 or an anti-PD-1 compound alone or in combination with a CTLA-4 inhibitor. The phase 2 portion enrolled only patients with treatment-naive metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. The primary endpoint of phase 1 was to find the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). We tested a novel regimen using four dose levels: oral pazopanib (600 or 800 mg daily on days 1-28, followed by a 7 day break) alternating with intravenous bevacizumab (5, 7·5, or 10 mg/kg, one on day 36 and one on day 50) on a 10-week cycle in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma naive to TKI treatment. The primary endpoint of phase 2 was median progression-free survival, assessed by a masked central statistician review. Dose selection (in patients who had completed 15 weeks) and activity (in patients who had completed one full 10-week cycle of the novel regimen) were analysed in the per-protocol population. Safety analyses included all patients who received any treatment. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01684397) and is ongoing but closed to new participants. Between Nov 21, 2012, and June 11, 2018, phase 1 enrolled 25 patients, with 18 patients evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity during the extended 15-week safety assessment period. The RP2D was established as pazopanib 800 mg daily (days 1-28) and bevacizumab 10 mg/kg on days 36 and 50 of a 10-week cycle. Between Jan 23, 2019, and Oct 19, 2023, phase 2 enrolled 53 patients, of whom 51 (including six from phase 1) were evaluable for activity and 59 were evaluable for safety. 36 (71%) patients were male and 15 (29%) were female, and 48 (94%) patients were White. 33 (65%) patients in phase 2 had favourable risk per the International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium categories. After a median follow-up of 63·7 months (IQR 16·2-73·5), median progression-free survival was 24·8 months (95% CI 17·2-34·3). The most common grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were hypertension (20 [34%] of 59) and elevated aspartate aminotransferase (seven [12%]) and alanine aminotransferase (ten [17%]). Five (8%) patients discontinued the study for drug-related serious adverse events. No treatment-related deaths occurred. The phase 1 portion identified the safe RP2D. The phase 2 portion showed that this novel regimen has promising antitumour activity in patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma in the predominantly favourable risk group who are naive to treatment. Phase 3 randomised controlled trial data are needed to confirm these findings. The Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center (RPCCC), US National Cancer Institute (NCI), Novartis.

articles.title: Donor-aware multi-cohort single-cell analysis identifies an LXR-linked tubular cholesterol-handling state in membranous nephropathy with a coordinated five-gene lipid-remodeling signature across renal tumors.
articles.abstract: Membranous nephropathy (MN) is an immune-mediated glomerular disease in which sustained proteinuria exposes renal tubular epithelial cells to an abnormal filtered-protein load. The tubular metabolic response to this exposure remains incompletely characterized. We investigated whether MN is associated with a reproducible tubular cholesterol-handling transcriptional state and assessed its relationship to protein overload in vitro. We further evaluated whether an experimentally anchored five-gene subset showed a coordinated tumor-associated transcriptional shift across major renal cancer histologies. Three kidney single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets and one glomerular bulk-transcriptomic cohort were analyzed using the donor as the biological replicate. GSE241302 was used for complete-case exploratory discovery, OEP004186 for formal donor-aware support, GSE171458 for directional support, and GSE200828 for tissue-level disease context. A frozen 47-gene LXR-linked cholesterol-handling program and its nested 37-gene cholesterol transport/efflux component were evaluated by donor-level pseudobulk analysis, leave-one-donor-out and leave-one-gene-out sensitivity analyses. HK-2 cells were exposed to protein overload, followed by quantitative reverse-transcription PCR for representative transport and lipid-remodeling genes. The same experimentally anchored five-gene panel was then evaluated in 129 paired tumor-adjacent-normal samples across TCGA-KIRC, TCGA-KIRP, and TCGA-KICH to define a renal tumor-associated lipid-remodeling context. Across all 3 MN donors in GSE241302, program scores were higher than the internal reference in proximal tubule (PT) and loop-of-Henle/thick ascending limb (loop/TAL) compartments. In OEP004186, the program was increased in PT (effect +0.480, false-discovery rate [FDR] 0.0128), PT-VCAM1 (+0.348, FDR 0.0165), and loop/distal epithelial cells (+0.310, FDR 0.0242), with positive effects in every leave-one-MN-donor-out analysis. GSE171458 provided concordant directional support in PT and loop/TAL. The PT-VCAM1 fraction was not increased in MN, whereas the program remained higher within both PT and PT-VCAM1, favoring a within-state transcriptional change. Sixteen program genes showed positive average effects across the three single-cell resources. In GSE200828, the overall program was higher in MN than in living donors (+0.226, FDR 0.0349) but not higher than in other glomerular diseases. Protein overload increased ABCA1, ABCG1, SREBF1, FASN, and SCD expression in HK-2 cells. Across the three renal cancer histologies, the five-gene panel showed a concordant paired increase (REML-pooled effect +0.967, 95% CI 0.843-1.092), and 85.3% of patients exhibited simultaneous increases in the cholesterol-efflux and lipid-synthesis/remodeling arms. MN is associated with a donor-supported LXR-linked cholesterol-handling transcriptional state concentrated in PT and loop/TAL-related epithelial compartments. The state is responsive to protein overload in HK-2 cells and may reflect a broader tubular lipid-homeostasis response to proteinuric kidney injury. The data do not establish direct LXR activation, increased cholesterol-efflux flux, or MN specificity. The paired renal cancer analysis further identifies a coordinated tumor-associated five-gene lipid-remodeling signature across KIRC, KIRP, and KICH, while not establishing tumor-cell-intrinsic LXR activation, immune effects, or a causal tumor mechanism.
